text: Remember Wren? Wren found a cave full of pentaja... and the money of a whole village stopped working.
Wren is made up. But again and again in history, money has had a Wren. A stone wheel. A glass bead. A seashell. A silver coin. Each time, someone found a cheaper way to make more of it.
This is: Every Wren in History.

Our first stop is Yap, a small island in the western Pacific. Yap has no good stone for making money. So for generations, Yapese sailors crossed hundreds of kilometres of open ocean, to the islands of Palau.
There, with tools made of shell, they carved limestone into great wheels with a hole in the middle. They called them rai. Then they hauled them home, on canoes and rafts. Not everyone made it back.

Every rai cost a dangerous voyage, so there were never many. That's what made them precious: their size, the whiteness of the stone, and how few ever made it home. A stone about two feet across could buy a big pig, or fifty baskets of food.

text: The biggest stones were far too heavy to move. So nobody moved them. When one changed hands, everyone just remembered who owned it now. One family's fortune was a stone at the bottom of the sea, lost in a storm generations earlier. The village still counted it.

Then, in eighteen seventy-one, an Irish-American captain called David O'Keefe was shipwrecked on Yap. He came back with a sailing ship and iron tools, and made the islanders an offer: he would bring their stones home from Palau, in exchange for dried coconut.

text: Stones that had been rare in eighteen forty became common. By nineteen twenty-nine, there were more than thirteen thousand on the island. The biggest were twelve feet across.
cap: Stones that had been rare in 1840 became common. By 1929, there were more than 13,000 on the island. The biggest were 12 feet across.

text: Sound familiar? It's Wren's cave, all over again. But this time, the islanders noticed. By later accounts, O'Keefe's stones, easy to get and suddenly everywhere, traded for LESS than the old ones. Yap had spotted its Wren.

On Yap, everyone knew each stone's story, so new stones could be priced lower, and old savings stayed safe. In Ulm Hollow, a pentaja is a pentaja: Wren's cave made everyone's pentaja worth less. Yap's money had a memory. Most money doesn't.
